The `package()` function is irrelevant here due to `--noprepare` and `--nobuild`, so it does not affect this narrow gate.

Fetching and sourcing this PKGBUILD will not execute any untrusted code or exfiltrate data. The operations performed by `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` and `makepkg --printsrcinfo` are limited to downloading declared sources and parsing the script, which is safe in this case.
</details>

The content defines a single source for the `drydock-bin` package, specifying that it should track the latest release from the GitHub repository `yetidevworks/drydock` using the `v` prefix.

This configuration is consistent with standard usage of nvchecker in AUR packages, where maintainers set up automatic version checking from an upstream GitHub repository. There are no network requests, executable commands, or file operations present. The file contains only declarative configuration and does not execute any code.

The use of `use_latest_release = true` is normal and expected for version tracking. There is no evidence of obfuscation, malicious payloads, or unauthorized data exfiltration. The source points to what appears to be the legitimate upstream project repository.

<details>
The PKGBUILD fetches prebuilt binaries from the project's official GitHub repository and verifies them using hardcoded SHA-256 checksums. The sources are correctly scoped to the declared upstream (https://github.com/yetidevworks/drydock), and the release binaries are downloaded over HTTPS from GitHub's release infrastructure, which is a trusted distribution channel. The package installs the binary, README, and license into standard system paths with appropriate permissions.

All checksums are provided and non-empty, indicating integrity verification for each downloaded file. The build process does not execute any unverified scripts, perform network requests beyond sourcing the defined URLs, or modify system state outside the package directory. There are no obfuscated commands, eval usage, or suspicious operations such as data exfiltration or dynamic code fetching. The use of `install` to place files in `/usr/bin`, `/usr/share/doc`, and `/usr/share/licenses` follows standard Arch Linux packaging practices.

While the version is tagged via `_gitversion=v${pkgver}` and relies on a GitHub release tag, this is normal for bin packages. The source URLs point to specific release artifacts and static files (README, LICENSE) at the tagged version, ensuring reproducibility. No VCS operations (like git clone or pull) occur during build, so there is no risk of unchecked code injection at build time.
</details>
